entries.root_cause: The first G10 membership guardrail validated only the presence of pg_auth_members lookup tokens, so a non-effectful query could satisfy the scope validator while leaving privileged membership escalation usable.
The expired-sync discovery guardrail checked dispatching and expiry markers independently, allowing an impossible conjunction that mentioned both states without providing a reachable recovery branch.
The Incident-create serialization guardrail proved that an advisory lock existed but not that it executed before the idempotency lookup, so concurrent creators could still race before serialization.
The transition replay guardrail checked conflict and target markers without proving control-flow order, allowing duplicate success to occur before an unreachable contradictory-target rejection.
The Alert timestamp guardrail accepted opened_at anywhere and rejected only an exact unqualified created_at sequence, allowing a qualified nonexistent created_at reference to be aliased as opened_at.

The strengthened membership guard still proved only that some v_role was checked, not that all three named G10 privileged roles were enumerated, allowing executor or invoker membership paths to escape validation.
The expired-claim validator proved predicate shape but not executable reachability, so a matching recovery branch could be placed after an unconditional return or inside a statically false branch.

The create-serialization validator compared source offsets but did not prove the advisory lock was executable, allowing a lock inside dead code to appear before the replay lookup while preserving the race.
The transition replay validator proved textual order inside a matching block but not reachability of that block, so contradictory replay rejection could remain dead code.
The Alert timestamp guard rejected created_at aliases but still accepted any expression aliased as opened_at, allowing fabricated opening timestamps such as resolved_at or transaction time.

The privileged-role loop and membership guard were validated independently, so the exact three-role loop could be empty while the effectful membership check executed afterward against only the final v_role value.
Reachability validation rejected returns and static-false branches but not an unconditional RAISE EXCEPTION before worker discovery, allowing recovery code to remain permanently unreachable.
The Alert timestamp provenance guard rejected AS aliases but not PostgreSQL aliases without AS, allowing resolved_at opened_at to masquerade as the canonical Alert opening timestamp.
The opened_at provenance guard validated only the outer select list and could be bypassed by a nested derived table that fabricated opened_at from resolved_at before the outer projection.
The privileged membership guard was required inside the correct role loop but could still sit inside a statically false branch, making the attestation textually present yet never executable.

Worker recovery reachability recognized only RAISE EXCEPTION and missed other unconditional PL/pgSQL RAISE forms such as RAISE SQLSTATE, allowing execution to terminate before expired-claim discovery.
The reachability helper treated every prior RAISE as unconditional, so a legitimate conditional role-safety exception incorrectly invalidated the later membership guard.

Expression blacklisting could not prove opened_at lineage, so nested expressions such as COALESCE(resolved_at,resolved_at) AS opened_at could still masquerade as the canonical Alert opening timestamp.
The recovery validator proved the pending/expired predicate existed but did not prove the matched row populated the value returned to the worker, allowing recovery to be evaluated and discarded.
The replay guard accepted IF FOUND text without proving FOUND was set by the required transition lookup for the same tenant, incident, and logical action.

Worker recovery validation found the pending/expired predicates but did not prove they were the effective tenant-scoped WHERE condition, so an always-false dominating filter could make the returned candidate set empty.
Privileged-role membership validation checked loop containment but not unconditional loop control transfers before the guard, allowing CONTINUE to skip validation for every role.
Incident-create serialization validation proved lock ordering textually but did not prove the lock dominates the equivalence lookup on the normal valid-input path.
Transition replay validation bound lookup and FOUND textually but did not prove the entire lookup/conflict block was reachable on the main transition path.
The scope validator attested only the first matching validated function definition, allowing a later CREATE OR REPLACE of the same function name to replace the safe implementation after attestation.
Worker discovery validation matched the canonical recovery predicate as a prefix rather than proving it was the complete effective filter, so a trailing AND FALSE could disable all discovery.

Membership validation rejected only known static-false forms and loop control transfers, but still allowed the fail-closed guard to be nested under an arbitrary condition that never matches the protected roles.
Incident-create serialization proved the advisory lock was outside IF branches but did not prove it was outside nonexecuting loops, allowing lookup to run without serialization.
Worker discovery validation proved the effective filter but not that rows originated from the canonical itsm.incident_sync_outbox relation, allowing fabricated derived rows to satisfy attestation.

Privileged-role membership validation found the exact loop anywhere in SQL text but did not prove it was inside an executing installation DO block, allowing a never-called function to carry the guard.

The advisory-lock validator only required the logical-action parameter to appear in the lock expression, allowing nondeterministic entropy to produce different lock keys for equivalent concurrent creates.
Function-block delimitation was case-sensitive even though PostgreSQL keywords are case-insensitive, allowing a lowercase decoy definition to bleed canonical evidence into the unsafe function block.
The reachability helper treated any preceding RAISE as an unconditional terminator, rejecting legitimate fail-fast validation branches even when the canonical discovery query remained reachable.

Worker discovery reachability rejected dead IF branches but did not reject the canonical candidate query when nested inside a nonexecuting loop, allowing discovery to be textually present yet unreachable.
Advisory-lock recognition operated on raw SQL text, so a canonical lock statement inside a line comment could satisfy attestation even though PostgreSQL would not execute it.
Validated-function uniqueness counted only CREATE OR REPLACE definitions, allowing DROP FUNCTION followed by plain CREATE FUNCTION of the same signature to replace the attested implementation.
SQL comment stripping was not quote-aware, so `--` inside a string literal could truncate subsequent executable text and hide forbidden cross-domain mutations from attestation.
Validated-function provenance rejected duplicate/drop-recreate definitions but not ALTER FUNCTION rename swaps that could install an unsafe decoy body under the validated name.
Worker discovery was protected against static-false and loop nesting but could still be placed inside an arbitrary IF branch not taken on the normal valid-input path.
The membership guard itself was top-level inside the extracted loop, but the exact three-role loop could still be nested under an unreachable IF in the executing DO block.
Transition replay equivalence rejected dead IF placement but did not reject the canonical replay lookup/conflict block when nested inside a nonexecuting loop.
The SQL comment lexer preserved single/double-quoted strings but not tagged dollar-quoted literals, allowing `--` inside `$tag$...$tag$` to truncate later executable SQL during attestation.
Validated-function provenance only recognized schema-qualified DDL, allowing unqualified DROP/CREATE under `SET search_path=itsm` to replace the attested implementation.
The privileged-role membership preflight could execute correctly and then be invalidated by a later role-membership GRANT, so installation final state no longer matched the attested safety invariant.
Advisory-lock attestation searched executable text but did not require the lock token to be an actual PERFORM call outside string literals, so literal contents could spoof serialization evidence.

Validated function extraction stopped only at the next qualified `itsm.` function definition, allowing an unqualified decoy function under search_path to bleed canonical evidence into an unsafe validated body.
Post-preflight membership mutation detection did not account for PostgreSQL's optional GROUP keyword on GRANT/REVOKE recipients, allowing protected roles to gain membership after attestation.

The SQL comment lexer handled ordinary quoted strings but not PostgreSQL escape strings, so an escaped quote could prematurely terminate lexical state and hide later executable SQL behind apparent comment syntax.
Validated-function detection did not recognize quoted canonical schema/function identifiers, allowing a quoted replacement of the same PostgreSQL object to escape occurrence/provenance checks.
Static validated-definition checks could be bypassed by dynamically constructing DROP/CREATE FUNCTION statements with PL/pgSQL EXECUTE.
SQL block-comment stripping was not nesting-aware, so PostgreSQL-valid nested comments could expose text to attestation that remained commented at execution time.
Post-preflight membership mutation detection matched only unquoted protected-role recipients, while PostgreSQL quoted lowercase identifiers resolve to the same roles.
Worker discovery attestation matched canonical query text from SQL literal contents instead of proving those statements were executable code.

Protected-role recipient matching required immediate comma/semicolon/end after the role, allowing valid trailing membership options such as WITH ADMIN OPTION to bypass post-preflight mutation detection.
Incident-create lock dominance rejected only prior RETURN statements, so a top-level RAISE could terminate execution before the lock while still passing attestation.
Case-insensitive matching also applied to quoted PostgreSQL identifiers, even though quoted names preserve case and therefore can denote non-canonical schemas/functions.
Post-preflight membership fencing covered GRANT/REVOKE but not equivalent membership-changing DDL such as CREATE ROLE ... IN ROLE/ROLE/ADMIN or ALTER GROUP ... ADD/DROP USER.

Quoted-identifier exact-case validation only covered fully quoted schema+function pairs, allowing mixed quoted/unquoted qualifiers such as "ITSM".g10_next_sync_candidate to masquerade as canonical lowercase objects.
Post-preflight membership scanning began after the enclosing DO block rather than immediately after the validated membership loop, allowing membership mutation in the remainder of that same DO block.
Worker discovery reachability recognized IF and LOOP nesting but not PL/pgSQL CASE, allowing canonical discovery evidence to live only in a nonexecuting CASE branch.
The SQL lexer preserved tagged dollar-quoted literals but not valid untagged $$...$$ literals, so comment markers inside a bare-dollar string could hide later executable mutations from analysis.

Validated-function identity checks rejected drops and renames but did not forbid ALTER FUNCTION/ROUTINE ... SET SCHEMA, allowing an attested canonical function to be moved out of the required itsm schema after validation.

Worker candidate validation proved that the canonical sync-outbox relation and filter both appeared, but allowed arbitrary row-eliminating joins between them, so a syntactically canonical query could be permanently empty.

Post-preflight GRANT/REVOKE detection recognized quoted protected recipients but only unquoted role identifiers on the granted/revoked side, allowing quoted role names to recreate forbidden membership edges.

Tagged dollar-quote delimiters were always treated as opaque literals, even when introduced by AS for a PL/pgSQL function body, allowing commented-out canonical evidence inside tagged procedural bodies to remain visible to later regex validation.

Validated-function rename fencing covered ALTER FUNCTION but not PostgreSQL's equivalent ALTER ROUTINE form, allowing rename-away/rename-into swaps to replace a canonical implementation without rejection.

Post-preflight membership patterns assumed a protected role would be the first element of a GRANT/REVOKE role or recipient list, allowing protected roles later in comma-separated lists to create forbidden membership edges.
Membership-preflight reachability rejected IF and LOOP nesting but omitted CASE, allowing the exact role loop or guard to exist only in a nonexecuting CASE branch.
Incident-create advisory-lock reachability rejected IF and LOOP nesting but omitted CASE, allowing the canonical lock call to be present only in a nonexecuting CASE branch.
Transition replay reachability rejected IF and LOOP nesting but omitted CASE, allowing the canonical lookup/conflict block to be present only in a nonexecuting CASE branch.

Incident-create lock reachability rejected IF, CASE, and LOOP nesting but did not distinguish EXCEPTION handlers, allowing the canonical advisory lock to exist only on an exceptional path that does not dominate the normal equivalence lookup.

Transition replay reachability invalidated only earlier RETURN statements and did not reuse the unconditional terminator analysis, allowing a top-level RAISE to terminate before replay equivalence while attestation still passed.

Exception-handler reachability considered only the innermost BEGIN frame, so a nested ordinary block inside an enclosing EXCEPTION handler could hide the canonical advisory lock on an exceptional-only path.

Worker reachability helpers analyzed unmasked function text, allowing control-flow tokens embedded in string literals such as 'END IF;' to alter nesting depth and make dead discovery code appear top-level reachable.
Membership-guard reachability rejected only bare EXIT/CONTINUE statements, allowing conditional EXIT WHEN/CONTINUE WHEN before the guard to skip privileged-role validation.

Membership GRANT/REVOKE classification searched for the token ON anywhere in the statement text, so a quoted role named "ON" was mistaken for an object-privilege clause and bypassed protected-role mutation detection.

Comment stripping assumed standard-conforming ordinary string semantics, so disabling standard_conforming_strings could make backslash-escaped quotes keep comment markers inside literals while the validator misclassified following executable SQL as a comment.

Privileged-role membership reachability rejected IF/CASE/LOOP nesting but did not reject EXCEPTION-handler confinement, allowing the canonical guard to exist only on an exceptional path that never runs during normal installation.

Incident-create lock evidence used a literal-masked view, but the equivalence lookup still scanned unmasked function text, allowing canonical lookup SQL inside a dollar-quoted literal to satisfy idempotency attestation without executing.

Transition replay matching and reachability scanned unmasked function text, allowing the complete canonical replay lookup/conflict block inside a dollar-quoted literal to satisfy attestation while runtime bypassed replay equivalence.

The string-semantics fence covered SET standard_conforming_strings but not executable set_config calls that mutate the same GUC, allowing ordinary-string lexing assumptions to diverge from PostgreSQL runtime semantics.

Membership-guard reachability used a literal-masked view, but the guard pattern itself still matched unmasked loop text, allowing the canonical guard inside a dollar-quoted literal to satisfy preflight attestation without executing.

Cross-domain mutation fencing covered only a narrow subset of DML/CREATE forms and unquoted schemas, leaving TRUNCATE, DROP, ALTER, MERGE and quoted canonical schema names able to mutate resources outside the authorized G10 boundary.

The set_config fence recognized only single-quoted standard_conforming_strings arguments, while PostgreSQL also accepts dollar-quoted text arguments that mutate the same GUC and desynchronize lexer assumptions from runtime semantics.

Incident Alert projection semantics were validated against unmasked function text, allowing the canonical alerting.alert query inside a dollar-quoted literal to satisfy provenance attestation without executing.
Cross-domain mutation fencing covered common DML, TRUNCATE and DDL forms but omitted relation-targeted COPY FROM, allowing direct writes into read-only external domains.

The final privileged-role preflight fenced membership changes but not post-preflight ALTER ROLE/USER attribute escalation, allowing protected runtime roles to gain SUPERUSER or equivalent authority after attestation.
set_config target matching recognized only literal spellings, allowing computed text expressions to mutate standard_conforming_strings while evading static attestation.

The final privileged-role preflight fenced membership and attribute changes but allowed creation of a protected runtime role after the loop, enabling a role absent from pg_roles during preflight to be installed later with excessive authority.
Cross-domain DML fencing required schema qualification immediately after UPDATE, DELETE FROM, or MERGE INTO and omitted PostgreSQL's optional ONLY modifier.
Cross-domain mutation fencing assumed explicitly qualified targets, while a mutable search_path could redirect otherwise-unqualified DML into protected external schemas.

The mutable-session fence recognized only unquoted set_config function names, while PostgreSQL resolves the lowercase quoted identifier "set_config" to the same function and can still alter resolution semantics.
The mutable target-resolution fence blocked SET search_path but not PostgreSQL's equivalent SET SCHEMA alias, allowing an unqualified DML target to resolve into a protected external schema.

Post-preflight protected-role creation fencing covered CREATE ROLE and CREATE USER but omitted PostgreSQL's CREATE GROUP role-creation alias, allowing a protected runtime principal to be created with excessive attributes after attestation.

Cross-domain mutation fencing rejected direct DML and DDL but did not reject mutation-capable object privilege grants, allowing a G10 runtime role to acquire direct write authority over protected external-domain relations without containing cross-domain DML in the installation artifact.

Mutable-context scanning treated canonical function-level SET search_path clauses, transaction-local jlmirror.tenant_id set_config calls, trigger EXECUTE FUNCTION syntax, and EXECUTE object privileges as if they were unsafe session-level or dynamic execution statements, making the scope validator reject the canonical G10 SQL it must attest.
Worker candidate attestation required no syntax between the canonical sync-outbox source and WHERE, rejecting the canonical tenant-bound join to itsm.incident that supplies the provider payload.

Protected-role preflight attestation required only the membership guard and failed to require the canonical unsafe-attribute guard covering login, superuser, database/role creation, inheritance, replication, and bypass-RLS capabilities.

The protected-role list was inferred by extracting quoted substrings from an arbitrary IN expression, so concatenated expressions could preserve the expected substrings while evaluating to nonexistent role names and skipping the preflight.

The standard_conforming_strings fence enumerated only OFF/FALSE spellings, while PostgreSQL accepts additional false boolean forms such as 0 and NO that can desynchronize quote/comment lexing from runtime semantics.

Cross-domain authority fencing covered relation write privileges but not CREATE or ALL privileges on protected external schemas, allowing a G10 runtime role to gain object-creation authority inside another domain.

Incident create replay attestation only searched for the logical_action_id comparison somewhere in the lookup statement, allowing contradictory predicates such as WHERE FALSE to make the replay lookup permanently empty while still passing.
Protected-role membership attestation accepted unqualified PostgreSQL catalog relations, allowing pg_temp shadowing to hide real role or membership rows from the installation preflight.

Incident create replay attestation verified the exact equivalence key but not that the replay lookup itself remained top-level reachable, allowing a dead conditional block to preserve syntax while bypassing duplicate/conflict handling.

Cross-domain DDL fencing matched CREATE INDEX as though the external schema immediately followed INDEX, while PostgreSQL identifies the mutated relation after ON, allowing index creation against protected external-domain relations.

Cross-domain DDL fencing covered direct relation DDL and CREATE INDEX target relations but omitted relation-attached trigger, rule, and policy DDL whose mutated relation is named after ON. A G10 hardening artifact could therefore attach behavior to protected external-domain relations without being rejected.
